Booking a Meeting Slot
Book your group’s seminar meeting in the online planner:
Book a meeting slot



One slot per group per week. Each slot takes up to three participants, and all of them must belong to the same group. Every group member who attends signs up for the same slot. Do not join a slot that a member of another group has already booked.

Monday slots: in person or online. You choose whether we meet in room HB-108 or via Zoom. After booking, send an email to dominik.liebl@ku.de stating which option your group wants.

Tuesday slots: online only. All Tuesday meetings take place via Zoom. No email is needed.

title: Statistics Seminar
text:
Seminar Rules


Groups: two to three students each.

Grading:

80% seminar thesis
20% presentation, in which every group member speaks.



Seminar thesis:


Length: 8–12 pages main text, including figures and tables; title page, table of contents, references, and appendix do not count.

Format: PDF with 12 pt font, 1.5 line spacing, and 2.5 cm margins. The thesis templates (Chapter 2) already meet these requirements.

Code: Only short snippets in the main text. Submit the full code separately so that all results can be reproduced (fixed random seed).

Submission: thesis.pdf and a ZIP file of your complete thesis folder (text, code, and literature). Deadline: TBA.



Exam registration (via campus.KU) deadline: January 21.

title: 3  Writing the Seminar Thesis
section: 3.2 Main Part 1: The Model and the Method
text:
3.2 Main Part 1: The Model and the Method


The model. Describe the data and the statistical model. What do we want to estimate or test?
The assumptions. List all assumptions of the method. Explain each assumption in words.
The method. Define the method with formulas and explain the idea behind it in words.
The theory. State the most important theoretical properties (e.g., unbiasedness, consistency, size and power of a test). Explain which assumptions are needed for them.

title: 2  Writing the Seminar Thesis
section: 2.3 Main Part 2: Applying the Method to Artificial Data
text:
2.3 Main Part 2: Applying the Method to Artificial Data
In a Monte Carlo simulation, you generate artificial data yourself. Therefore, you know the truth and can check how well the method works.


All assumptions hold. Generate data for which all assumptions hold. Check that the method works as the theory says.
One assumption is violated. Change the data so that one assumption is violated (e.g., heavy tails, heteroskedasticity, small samples). Violate only one assumption at a time.
Different sample sizes. Repeat each simulation for several sample sizes \(n\).
Measure the performance, for instance:

estimators: bias, variance, and mean squared error,
confidence intervals: coverage probability and average length,
tests: empirical size and power.

Report the results in tables and plots, and explain them in words: When does the method work well? When does it fail?

title: 2  Writing the Seminar Thesis
section: 2.4 Main Part 3: Applying the Method to Real Data
text:
2.4 Main Part 3: Applying the Method to Real Data


Describe the data set: Where does it come from? What are the variables?
Apply the method to the data and interpret the results.
Check the assumptions: Are they plausible for these data? What does your simulation study (Main Part 2) tell you about how much you can trust the results?

title: 2  Writing the Seminar Thesis
text:
2.5 Conclusion
(max. 1 Page)


Summarize your main findings.
Give practical advice: When should a user apply the method, and what should a user be careful about?

title: 2  Writing the Seminar Thesis
text:
2.6 Thesis Templates
Choose one of the following two templates. Both already implement the formal requirements listed in the seminar rules.
Overleaf (LaTeX): Download the LaTeX thesis template. On Overleaf, choose New Project → Upload Project, upload the ZIP file, and share the project with your group members. You write the thesis together in the browser; no local LaTeX installation is needed. Overleaf cannot run R or Python: you run your simulation study (R/simulation.R) on your own computer, and it saves the tables and figures that you upload to the results/ folder of your Overleaf project. See the included README.md for details.
Quarto: Download the Quarto thesis template. It renders to PDF. It also shows how to keep code out of the PDF: the method is implemented in R/functions.R, the simulation study in R/simulation.R, and thesis.qmd only reads the saved simulation results to show tables and figures. See the included README.md for details.
